body:
We discussed the relation of private fields and this proxy in https://github.com/tc39/ecma262/pull/688 and https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1652868 and couldn't come up with a reasonable leak.

In your test case it looks like the parent window both sets and gets the private fields so there's not really any cross-origin communication happening, but maybe I'm missing something.

If I'm not missing something, perhaps we should at least state somewhere that this is considered a non-issue from a web platform perspective. (It might still be an issue for Fx specifically as discussed in the aforementioned bug.)

cc @mgaudet @evilpie @petervanderbeken @erights

I've been thinking about this for a while, and my personal preference would be that we should make some objects ineligible for private fields/methods, and throw a type error when attempting the super override trick on them. 

Cross origin objects such as Window and Location being my first two suggested targets.

This is opinion is heavily influenced by the fact that getting this *right* for Gecko is a very large amount of engineering work with very very low user value. I have a patch waiting on review to actually make these operations throw already prepared [here](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1726039)

As an aside: As I understand it, conceptually there's not problem with private fields and methods being stamped onto a cross origin object. The challenges are practical engineering ones. 

The mental model around a private field `class A { #x }` is supposed to be that the private 'field' doesn't really exist, but instead signifies a hidden weak map: So conceptually, adding a private field `#x`, with value `1` to an object `o` is the same as adding an entry in a hidden weak map associated with `A` and field `#x`, where `o` is the key, and `1` is the value. 

This means conceptually, stamping `#x` onto a cross-origin window is merely putting that window in a weak map as a key; which totally should work! 

It's just the engineering is a complicated mess, because `window` is a complicated object in browsers, represented depending on context, by multiple objects with weird semantics around navigation.

From the TC39 side I am personally quite happy to add a host carveout which lets hosts specify certain objects as ineligible for getting private fields, if that's the direction HTML wants to go. (I would volunteer to write and present the PR to plenary, even.)

I would prefer if the ability to prevent adding private fields through return override was also possible for user code. I have actually been wondering about adding a new options bag to `Object.create`, and an option which would set a slot on the newly created object that would be checked by [PrivateMethodOrAccessorAdd](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-privatemethodoraccessoradd) and fail if set.

Then all that HTML would need to do is set that slot on the objects it wants.

Edit: My motivation is that indeed private fields are equivalent to WeakMap, but now we've created an undeniable WeakMap implementation through syntax, where WeakMap is a deniable API.

> I would prefer if the ability to prevent adding private fields through return override was also possible for user code.

That's reasonable, but I think that proposed change would move through committee much slower, so I think the appropriate staging would be to first give the ability to hosts and, if we do in fact add this capability to userland, rephrase the host carveout in terms of that machinery at that point.
Strongly in favor of just disallowing this on window proxies and whatever other host objects we deem appropriate.
I'd like to avoid another `IsHTMLDDA` and there is motivation for this capability to not be host special behavior, but of course such a change would have to go through the committee process.

Thanks for the pointers and the pings.

> In your test case it looks like the parent window both sets and gets the private fields so there's not really any cross-origin communication happening

Right, it was only testing wether the parent window can mutate another window in a cross-origin browsing context, though only the parent window has actual access to these private members.

My intuition is that allowing the private access in this matter doesn't seem to be quite useful, AFAICT,  and since this is security-related, the fewer exceptional access there is, the better, even if we might not be able to find a probable risk for now.

From the HTML editor point of view, it feels a bit nicer if these objects aren't special in this regard. But, I care much less about that than I care about implementers having a good time. So I'm happy for implementers to guide our decision here, and when we have a decision, for them to work with TC39 on whatever hooks are necessary.
What's the next step for this? Should we work through TC39 to build the carveout, then do the HTML integration? or add normative text to HTML, and let TC39 catch up?
Working through TC39 to build the carveout seems better, as that has more veto points.

> From the TC39 side I am personally quite happy to add a host carveout which lets hosts specify certain objects as ineligible for getting private fields, if that's the direction HTML wants to go. (I would volunteer to write and present the PR to plenary, even.)

@bakkot if you want to do that, that would be awesome. If you don't have time, let me know, and I can try to take a stab at it.

ECMA262 PR: https://github.com/tc39/ecma262/pull/2807

I've put it on the agenda for July and will do my best to represent the positions expressed in this thread, though if @syg or someone else more familiar with WindowProxy and implementations wants to help present that would be appreciated.

Note that I've currently written it such that only _exotic_ objects can reject private fields, which includes WindowProxy and Location but not most other objects. If there's a compelling reason to relax that restriction I'm happy to do so, but I figured I'd write it with the smallest carveout necessary for the concerns expressed in this thread.

For the HTML side, does this make sense to also apply to `Location` objects (or perhaps just make a blanket rule about cross-origin objects)? 

We have some similar implementation challenges for Location objects.
With my HTML editor hat on I am OK with either including or excluding Location in the special-casing here.

The TC39 PR to enable a fix for this has just been merged here: https://github.com/tc39/ecma262/pull/2807 

HTML will now just need to provide an implementation of `HostEnsureCanAddPrivateElement`

The JS spec now has an affordance for this: [`HostEnsureCanAddPrivateElement`](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/abstract-operations.html#sec-hostensurecanaddprivateelement).

HTML can define `HostEnsureCanAddPrivateElement` to throw a TypeError when passed a WindowProxy and/or a Location object, and that will prevent private fields from being added to those objects.

I should note that we didn't want to precisely write down rules for what hosts were "allowed" to do with this hook, but it's added on the understanding that it's intended only for weird cross-realm edge cases like those two, not arbitrary objects. If it eventually proves to be the cases that there's a broader class of objects which require this facility, please ping TC39 again.
Great! @mgaudet or @joyeecheung, are you up for sending a HTML spec PR?
A leak is something that is unintentionally exposed. Intentionally exposing something isn't a leak.

@ljharb you said that in the mentioned thread ... it's kinda irrelevant if [a leak can be accidental or code around can make it accidental](https://es.discourse.group/t/js-class-fields-potentially-harmful/1616/47) ... if the PL exposes ways to leak for private fields, nothing any other PL does, I believe we can't blame developers here, but I am also not answering in two threads, as everything more with real-world examples is exposed in the one I've linked. I just would like to know what people in here, likely not following the other thread, think. Repeating your position around this topic might not be super-helpful for them, surely not for me, or yourself.
@WebReflection that doesn't demonstrate cross-origin communication as far as I can tell.

FWIW the OP was more about this inconsistency:

```js
new ClassWithPrivateField(cross_origin_iframe.contentWindow);  // Worked
cross_origin_iframe.contentWindow.foo = 'bar';  // SecurityError
```

And the fix is to make the first invocation throw as well.

In the example in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/7952#issuecomment-1435771570, `cross_origin_iframe.contentWindow.leak()`  should throw a SecurityError instead of returning 1 (accessing public properties, like `leak`, on cross-origin window proxies has always been checked, before and after class fields).

maybe I misunderstood the title of this discussion but my code was to demo that leaks can happen on the global object for private fields that have nothing to do with the global field ... if this was about something else then apologies I didn't realize it

I believe the original comment

> We discussed the relation of private fields and this proxy in https://github.com/tc39/ecma262/pull/688 and https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1652868 and couldn't come up with a reasonable leak.

meant that it is not possible to leak public properties (checked) through private fields (previously unchecked). The example https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/7952#issuecomment-1435771570, however, was doing it the other way around (trying to leak private fields using public properties), which is not going to work (throws a security error) either way because public properties are always checked for cross-origin window proxies. So it could not invalidate that original comment.

Sorry, upon a closer look I think the original comment was about memory leaks, not leaking access to the fields - though in any case, the subsequent patches that make private fields uninstallable on cross-origin window proxies would make either kind of leak even less viable.

I’ve mocked `cross_origin_iframe` as a plain object with a `contentWindow` field that’s also a plain object to demo generic leaks around private fields weird code could provide exposing these via a public field. If this was all about cross origin then of course my demo doesn’t invalidate that, it just validates that if this was a security/leak issue or concern for cross origin global contexts, it’s the same concern for everything else that’s not cross origin.

In that case I think that's a separate issue, since neither this (before the fix):

```js
new ClassWithPrivateField(cross_origin_iframe.contentWindow);  // Worked
cross_origin_iframe.contentWindow.foo = 'bar';  // SecurityError
```

nor this (after):

```js
new ClassWithPrivateField(cross_origin_iframe.contentWindow);  // SecurityError
cross_origin_iframe.contentWindow.foo = 'bar';  // SecurityError
```

can happen to plain objects.
